title: Linux Examples
description: Small Linux examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Find your place
examples.description: A terminal displays a shell, which reads commands. pwd prints the directory you are currently using.

examples.title: List files
examples.description: ls lists directory entries. The -a option includes names beginning with a dot, which are often hidden in normal views.

examples.title: Create and enter a folder
examples.description: mkdir creates a directory. cd changes the shell's current directory. Use a new name that does not replace existing work.

examples.title: Write and read a small file
examples.description: printf writes text. A redirection sign sends that text into a file. cat prints a file's contents.

examples.title: Append a line
examples.description: Two redirection signs append text to the end of a file. Earlier content stays in place.

examples.title: Copy a practice file
examples.description: cp makes another copy of a file. Give a new destination name when you want to preserve both versions.

examples.title: Search lines
examples.description: grep prints lines that match a pattern. With -F it treats the pattern as fixed text rather than a special pattern language.

examples.title: Count and sort
examples.description: wc counts things such as lines. sort writes lines in order to its output. Piping connects one command's output to another.

examples.title: Quote paths with spaces
examples.description: Quotes keep several words together as one shell argument. This matters when a path contains spaces.

examples.title: Inspect permissions
examples.description: Permissions describe who may read, write or execute a file. ls -l shows them along with other details.

examples.title: See running processes
examples.description: A process is a running program. ps shows information about selected processes without stopping them.

examples.title: Write a tiny shell script
examples.description: A script saves commands so you can run them again. This one only prints a greeting and the current path.
examples.code:
printf '#!/bin/sh
printf "Hello, learner\n"
pwd
' > hello.sh
sh hello.sh
